prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a discovery in the sense I care about: a concrete result measured in nature, resting on one clear idea. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift limits while keeping thousands of atoms interrogated at once, and Ye's group then drove accuracy and stability to the 1e-18 regime. Independent laboratories on several continents now confirm and compare these clocks, the redefinition of the second is being prepared around them, and they already deliver tests of constancy of fundamental constants, searches for ultralight dark matter and relativistic geodesy. The two credited names map cleanly onto concept-plus-demonstration and performance-record, so a two-person prize needs no arbitrary cut. Four of eight members placed B018 first, and the reasons they gave (Kroll on measurement-limited progress, Lindroth and Olsson on a clear invention with a stable interpretation) are scientific, not merely habitual.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the case rests on an anticipated consequence rather than a completed one, and the frequency-comb and ion-clock contributions that made 1e-18 comparisons possible were either already honoured or sit outside this credit. A further worry is that the prize would reward an incremental, if remarkable, refinement of atomic clocks whose conceptual novelty is narrower than that of IceCube opening a new messenger or Cirac and Zoller defining a field. Its natural audience is also narrower than that of the other leading candidates, and opening support from four first places could reflect similar instrument-oriented tastes in the room rather than superior merit.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first and placed optical lattice clocks only fifth, noting that the redefinition of the second is still pending, which could argue for waiting, and that the committee has already recognised the comb.
responses.response: I take the timing point seriously but do not think it is decisive: the scientific achievement, accuracy at 1e-18 reproduced in several laboratories, is established regardless of when the metrological bodies act, and a prize should follow the discovery, not a policy calendar. On the comb, the Hall and Hansch recognition covers a different invention; Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is not contained in it. I do agree with Pearce that IceCube is a strong case and I keep B007 as my first alternative. My remaining disagreement is attribution: Pearce finds the two-person Halzen and Karle configuration clean, but for a collaboration of several hundred I am less comfortable that two names fairly represent the leadership, whereas for B018 the attribution is unusually clear.

responses.point: Johansson ranked Cirac and Zoller first for the trapped-ion gate and quantum simulation proposals, arguing that experimental credit is partly covered by the 2012 prize so that a theory-only prize is coherent, and ranked optical lattice clocks seventh.
responses.response: I agree that Cirac and Zoller are original and have shaped several platforms, and I retain B032 as an alternative. But I resist treating a theory-only prize as obviously coherent here: the 1995 gate proposal was largely realised by experimentalists whose recognition in 2012 concerned a different achievement, so a prize for the proposals risks leaving the experimental discovery unrewarded and the citation abstract. I also doubt that a third quantum-information prize in a short span is the best use of a limited slot when optical lattice clocks have a measured, quantitative result. Where I concede ground is on maturity: three decades of confirmation makes B032 certainly ripe, and if the committee wants a pure-theory award it is the strongest such case on the list.

responses.point: Mehlig placed fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B002) first, as an original and conceptually clean framework now confirmed in optical tweezers and single-molecule experiments, with Crooks the most awkward omission among three laureates.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual quality of B002 and agree that the experiments with single molecules and colloids are a serious confirmation. My difficulty is attribution, which Mehlig himself identifies: Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks, Seifert and others made distinct and arguably equal contributions, and any three-name cut is likely to feel arbitrary. The tests also confirm exact mathematical identities more than they reveal a new phenomenon in nature, which is why I rank it below discoveries where a new capability or observation emerges. I would be prepared to move if colleagues argue that the experimental verification gives it more of a discovery character than I have credited.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B018 first as the clearest case of measurement-limited progress, with multiple independent laboratories confirming 1e-18 comparisons and a clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity and attribution reasoning, but I would qualify one thing: Kroll and I should be careful not to equate a clean two-person credit with scientific superiority, since a tidy list is also true of B032. What I add to his case is that the clock result is not only an accuracy record but a new capability, comparing clocks at 1e-18 turns gravitational redshift over millimetres into a measurement, and that is what justifies placing it ahead of other well-attributed candidates. Kroll's list also names other contributors, such as Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley, whose roles remain unresolved by the credit file; I would not want the citation to imply their work did not matter.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the pending redefinition of the second as a reason to wait or as incidental to the discovery.

How much weight to give contributors outside the credit, such as Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Bloom group, compared with Katori and Ye; I have not verified the priority sequence of early lattice-clock demonstrations.
Whether four first-place votes for B018 reflect shared tastes in instrumentation, which I should discount.
Collaboration-scale attribution for B007 remains unsettled and could change my ordering of the alternatives.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is tied to B018, B007 or B032, and my own research in string theory and cosmology does not overlap with these candidates.
